content_metadata.description: An educational video that explains how to balance chemical reactions using the trial and error method, featuring the presenter Paritosh Bhide.

qAndA.question: In the first example equation, how many atoms of Na are present on the reactant side?

qAndA.answer: Changing the formula would change the chemical compound itself. Balancing is done by adjusting the coefficients, not the chemical formulas.
qAndA.question: Why is the chemical formula for water not changed to H2O3 in the second example?
What is the name of the compound Al(OH)3?

qAndA.answer: It allows for systematic adjustments to the coefficients until the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides of the equation.
qAndA.question: Why is the trial and error method used for balancing equations?

qAndA.answer: It provides a clear and concise way to compare the number of atoms on both sides, making it easier to understand the concept of balancing chemical equations.
qAndA.question: How does the visual representation of the balanced equation and atom counts enhance the learning experience?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Balancing of a chemical reaction by trial and error method, step 1.
Write the chemical equation from the given word equation. For example, NaOH plus HCl gives N
SCl plus H2O. It is derived from sodium hydroxide plus hydrochloric acid gives sodium chloride
plus water.
Step 2. Compare the number of atoms of various elements present on the two sides of the
arrow, that is, of the equation. If it is the same, then the reaction is already balanced.
On the reactant side, Na has 1 atom and on the product side, it also has 1 atom. On the
reactant side, as well as the product side, O has 1 atom. H has 2 atoms, both on the reactant
as well as product side.
CL has 1 atom on the reactant side and 1 atom on the product side. Number of atoms of all
the elements on the reactant and product side are same, so the reaction is balanced.
ALCl3 plus H2O gives LOH thrice plus HCl. In this reaction, the total number of elements
on both sides are unequal, so the reaction is unbalanced. AL has 1 atom on both sides.
CL has 3 atoms on the reactant side, but only 1 on the product side. H has 2 atoms on
the reactant side, but 4 atoms on the product side. O has 1 atom on the reactant side, but
3 atoms on the product side.
Step 3. Start balancing an equation from the compound which contains maximum number of
atoms. Moreover, it is convenient to consider, first that element in the same compound, which
has unequal number of atoms on the two sides. Please remember that the formula of the compound
must remain the same, while balancing the number of atoms.
Select ALOH thrice for balancing. Number of AL on both sides are equal, so select oxygen
for balancing next. Initially, in the reactants, the number of oxygen is 1 and the number
of product is 3. So, to balance, we will multiply by 3 in the reactant side.
So the formula of H2O cannot be changed to H2O3. Instead, a coefficient of 3 will have
to be written before H2O. Such as ALCl3 plus 3H2O gives ALOH thrice plus HCl. Equation
is still not balanced as the number of H on both sides are not equal.
Initially, the number of hydrogen atoms on the reactant side is 6. While on the product
side, it is 4. So, to balance the equation, we need to add 2 more hydrogen atoms to the
product side.
So we shall multiply the HCl compound by 3, giving a reaction ALCl3 plus 3H2O gives ALOH thrice
plus 3HCl. Check if the equation is balanced or not. Now, all elements are equal on both
sides. It means that this equation is now a balanced chemical equation.
Step 4. Write down the final balanced equation again.
